screens.title: Delegated Execution, Local Actions, and Run Once
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore how Ansible can run a task somewhere other than the host you are currently iterating over. You will learn the purpose of delegated execution and the common patterns that rely on it, such as running control-node build steps, updating external services, or ensuring a single centralized action after a multi-host deployment. We will also show how run_once limits a task to a single execution in a batch, why inventory and delegated host variables differ, and how to use delegate_to: localhost as the modern replacement for local_action. These capabilities let you orchestrate complex workflows: prepare artifacts on the control node, copy them to many targets, and send one notification from the controller. As you learn, notice the safety and variable considerations, and how run_once interacts with batching or serial execution. By the end you will understand when to delegate, when to run locally, and when to prefer separate plays instead of delegation.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Delegation controls where a task runs; run_once controls how many times it runs. Use delegate_to and delegate_to: localhost to centralize actions while keeping the play focused on many targets.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Delegated Execution
Delegated Execution, Local Actions, and Run Once
Why moving where a task executes gives you central control and safer orchestration.
In this lesson
How to use delegate_to, run_once, and localhost actions to centralize steps like builds, notifications, and API calls.
Why it matters
Orchestration often needs a single authoritative executor. Delegation provides that without changing the play's target list.
Quick orientation

Delegation changes where a single task runs. run_once limits execution to one host. delegate_to: localhost runs a task on your control node so it can access local tools and files.

Visual concept
Centralize, delegate, distribute
Concept cards
Delegate specific tasks to a host that can perform them, such as a management server with cloud SDKs.
Run_once coordinates one-off steps like schema creation or a notification after a multi-host deployment.
Run local build steps on the control node using delegate_to: localhost, then distribute artifacts to many targets.
Explore Key Topics
delegate_to basics — pick a host for the task to run on.
run_once behavior — execute once per batch or delegated host.
control-node work — use localhost when you need local tools or files.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four concrete skills. First, you will understand the purpose of delegated execution: why and when you would run a task on a host other than the current target. This matters because many orchestration steps, like interacting with cloud APIs or updating a load balancer, must run from a host that has the right access or tools. Second, you will be able to use delegate_to correctly to run a single task on another host, and you will know inventory and connectivity requirements for the delegated host. Third, you will implement run_once so tasks execute only a single time per batch; you will learn how batching and serial execution affect which host runs that single task. Fourth, you will perform local control-node actions using delegate_to: localhost or local_action and know the security and cleanup considerations for these patterns. Each skill includes a practical example or mnemonic so you can see how to apply it in real playbooks.

screens.title: What is Delegated Execution?
screens.narratorSegment: Delegated execution means running a specific Ansible task on a different host than the play's current target. This is useful when the action requires tools, credentials, or network access that the original target does not have. For example, you might run cloud A P I calls from a management server, update a load balancer from the load balancer host, or create artifacts on the control node before copying them out. The directive delegate_to is the mechanism that instructs Ansible to open a connection to another host and execute the task there. Delegation keeps the play focused on the inventory host list so the loop semantics and registered variables remain consistent. Importantly, variables like inventory_hostname and ansible_host continue to refer to the original target, while ansible_delegated_host points to the host where the task actually ran. A common misconception is believing delegate_to changes the play's target; it does not. It only changes the execution context for that single task. Think of delegation as borrowing a worker to perform one job on behalf of the current target. When you plan orchestration, ask which host holds the necessary tools and where state should be recorded before deciding to delegate.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Delegated execution runs a task on a different host while preserving the play's original concept of the target host.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › What is Delegated Execution?
Core Concept
Delegated Execution

Delegated execution allows a task to run on a different host using delegate_to. It is useful when the delegated host has access to required tooling, credentials, or networks that the original inventory host lacks.

When to use it
Cloud API calls, load balancer updates, local packaging on the control node.
Misconception
delegate_to does not change the play's target list; it only changes where that task runs.
Annotated example
Imagine a task that registers a web server's IP with an external DNS service. The DNS client runs on a management host. Using delegate_to, the registration command executes on the DNS host, but it registers the IP of the original web server. Variables keep referring to the intended host, while the action executes where possible.
Example scenario
Add newly created webserver IP to load balancer via a task delegated to the load balancer host which has the load balancer API access.
Key Takeaway

Delegation is the tool to run a task where it can succeed without changing who the play manages.

screens.title: delegate_to: mechanics and requirements
screens.narratorSegment: The delegate_to directive tells Ansible to establish a connection to the named host and run the task there. For this to work the delegated host must be reachable from the control node and should be present in the inventory with the necessary connection variables. When Ansible executes a delegated task, it does not change the play's iteration target: the play still moves through the original hosts, and registered variables like inventory_hostname continue to refer to those original hosts. In the delegated task you gain access to a special variable, ansible_delegated_host, which holds the name of the host that actually executed the command. This distinction matters when you need to refer to facts of the original target versus the executor. For example, you might want to use the original host IP to register with a DNS service while performing the registration call from a management host. A frequent pitfall is assuming delegate_to will inherit facts from the original host; it will not. If you need facts from the original host within a delegated action, gather them beforehand and pass them as variables to the delegated task. Always confirm inventory entries and SSH keys for the delegated host before relying on delegation in production.

keyIdea.text: delegate_to opens a connection to the specified host to run the task; ansible_delegated_host shows where it ran while inventory variables still reference the original target.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › delegate_to mechanics
How it connects

When you set delegate_to: host_name, Ansible opens a connection to host_name and runs the task there. The delegated host must exist in your inventory or be reachable by the control node with appropriate connection variables. The play's loop still advances over the original hosts, so variables tied to inventory refer to the original target unless you explicitly use the delegated host variables.

Important variable behavior
inventory_hostname and ansible_host refer to the play's current inventory host. ansible_delegated_host refers to the host where the task executed. Use these intentionally.
Practical tip
If delegated task needs original-host facts, gather them first and pass as vars to the delegated action to avoid relying on implicit facts at runtime.
Example
Register a webserver IP with a DNS host. Use inventory_hostname to identify the webserver and delegate the API call to the DNS host, which performs the update.
Common mistake

Assuming delegated tasks automatically see the target's facts. They do not. Gather and pass facts when needed.

screens.title: Variables: inventory_hostname vs ansible_delegated_host
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding which variable refers to which host is essential when delegating tasks. inventory_hostname always points to the host that the play is iterating over, the host Ansible is conceptually managing in that task iteration. ansible_host typically holds the address used to contact that original host. When you delegate a task, the execution happens on a different machine; Ansible exposes ansible_delegated_host to indicate the actual executor. Use inventory_hostname and ansible_host when you need data about the original target, for example the IP address you want to register. Use ansible_delegated_host if you need to know where the command ran, for example to log execution location or to use facts from the delegated host. A common mistake is swapping these accidentally and recording the wrong host into an external system. If your task registers information about the original target, explicitly reference inventory_hostname or ansible_host in templates or A P I calls, even inside a delegated task. This clear separation prevents mixing up who is the subject of the action and who is the actor. Variables: inventory_hostname vs ansible_delegated_host means inventory_hostname and ansible_host describe the original target; ansible_delegated_host names the host that executed the task.. In practical terms, why these variables differ and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Variable semantics
Original target variables

inventory_hostname and ansible_host refer to the host the play is iterating over. Use these to refer to the subject of the task: the server you intend to manage or register in external systems.

Use case
Register the original host IP with DNS using ansible_host inside a delegated DNS update task.
Delegated host variable

ansible_delegated_host tells you where the delegated task actually executed. Use it to log or conditionalize behavior that depends on the executor host.

Use case
If you need to record which management node performed an API call, capture ansible_delegated_host in the result or log output.
Scenario
A play iterates webservers. A task delegates a DNS update to dns_host. To add the webserver IP, refer to ansible_host of the original; to note which dns_host executed it, read ansible_delegated_host. Mixing these up will register the wrong host in DNS or misattribute actions in logs.
Key Takeaway

Keep subject and executor variables separate: subject uses inventory variables, executor uses ansible_delegated_host.

screens.title: run_once: ensure a single execution
screens.narratorSegment: The run_once directive tells Ansible to execute a task only once within the current batch of hosts. If you target multiple hosts in a single play, a task with run_once: true runs only for the first host in that batch. This behavior is particularly useful for tasks that must run a single time, such as generating a unique deployment ID, creating a global resource, or sending an external notification. When combined with delegate_to, run_once controls how many times the delegated action happens: you can delegate a single notification to the control node and ensure it only runs once, for example. A key subtlety is that run_once is applied per batch, and batching changes the identity of the first host. If you use serial or a dynamic inventory, the first host may differ between runs, so plan accordingly. A common misconception is expecting run_once to run on a fixed host across runs; instead it runs on the first host seen in the current execution ordering. If you need a specific host to run a one-time task always, explicitly delegate_to that host and include run_once to avoid accidental repeats.

keyIdea.title: run_once semantics
keyIdea.text: run_once executes a task only once per batch, and should be used with awareness of batching, serial, and delegation to guarantee consistent behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › run_once behavior
What run_once does

When you set run_once: true on a task, Ansible will run that task only once for the current batch of hosts. If your play targets many hosts in one batch, it runs on the first host in the batch. Combined with delegate_to you can control both who is the subject and who executes the action.

Use case
Generate a unique deployment id on the control node once, register it, and share it with all hosts.
Subtlety
If you use serial or batching, the 'first host' can change. For guaranteed host identity, combine run_once with delegate_to: specific_host.
Concrete example
Create a deployment ID on localhost with run_once: true and set it as a fact so all hosts share the same id.
Key Takeaway

run_once is for one-time operations, but ordering and batching determine which host executes it.

screens.title: delegate_to: localhost vs local_action
screens.narratorSegment: Historically Ansible provided local_action as a shorthand to run a task on the control node. Today, delegate_to: localhost is the preferred and more explicit approach. Both achieve the same effect: the task executes on the control node, which is useful for creating local build artifacts, calling local tools, or performing cleanup. The advantage of delegate_to: localhost is consistent syntax with other delegate_to uses and clearer intent when scanning a playbook. When running locally, remember the control node's security posture: tasks executed there have access to local files and credentials. Also, local_action or delegate_to: localhost will not magically copy remote facts to the controller; if you need facts from remote hosts while running local operations, gather them first and pass them explicitly. A mistake students often make is assuming local actions are isolated; in reality they can expose secrets or leave temporary files on the control node if you do not clean them up. Use run_once with delegate_to: localhost when you want a single controller-side step in a multi-host deployment. delegate_to: localhost vs local_action means use delegate_to: localhost for control-node tasks; local_action is deprecated shorthand but both run on the controller.. In practical terms, preferred syntax and behavioral equivalence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › localhost execution
delegate_to: localhost

This is the preferred form to run tasks on the control node. It is explicit and consistent with other delegate_to usage, making playbooks easier to read and maintain.

Use cases
Local builds, packaging, interacting with local cloud CLIs, and centralized notifications.
local_action

local_action is an older shorthand equivalent to delegate_to: localhost, but the latter is clearer. Prefer delegate_to for consistency.

Security note
Tasks running on the controller can access local secrets. Clean up temporary files and minimize sensitive operations on the control node when possible.
Practical tip
Combine delegate_to: localhost with run_once: true when you want a single controller-side action during a multi-host run, for example creating a build artifact only once.

screens.title: Walkthrough: delegated_deploy.yml starter playbook
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the provided delegated_deploy. yml example to see delegation and run_once in action. The play targets webservers while creating a temporary build directory on the control node using delegate_to: localhost and run_once: true. That ensures the directory is created only once, on the controller, even though the play iterates multiple web servers. Next, a simulated copy creates a package in that directory again delegated to the control node. Notice the tasks that run on remote hosts do not use delegate_to and run on each webserver. The play sets facts based on a control node command that generates a deployment ID with delegate_to: localhost and run_once, then the set_fact runs on each host so they share the same ID. Later the play copies the package from the control node's registered path to each remote host and unarchives it remotely. Finally, a centralized debug notification runs delegate_to: localhost with run_once to ensure a single, controller-sent message, and cleanup removes the temporary directory if it was created. This pattern keeps builds centralized while distributing the artifact to all targets. keyIdea.text: Create artifacts on the controller once, distribute to all hosts, and run a single centralized post-deploy action using delegation and run_once.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Starter playbook walkthrough
Key task sequence
  1. Create build dir on control node with delegate_to: localhost and run_once: true so the directory exists only once.
  2. Simulate package creation on the controller, also delegated and run once, registering the package path.
  3. Ensure remote deployment directory exists on each webserver, run per-host.
  4. Copy package from controller path to each webserver and unarchive remotely.

- name: Delegated Deployment Workflow

        path: "/tmp/app_build_{{ ansible_date_time.iso8601_basic_short }}"
        state: directory
        mode: '0755'
      delegate_to: localhost
      run_once: true
      register: build_dir_result

    - name: Simulate application build and package creation on control node
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        content: "This is the application content for version 1.0
"

screens.title: Process: local build then distribute
screens.narratorSegment: This process outlines the common orchestration pattern of building once on the control node and distributing to many hosts. Step one: create a temporary build directory on the control node using delegate_to: localhost and run_once so it happens exactly once. Step two: generate or copy the build artifact into that directory on the controller, again using run_once to avoid repeated builds. Step three: iterate over each target host to ensure the remote deployment directory exists and prepare the host for receiving artifacts. Step four: copy the artifact from the controller to each host using the registered path. Because the artifact was created on localhost, the copy must reference the controller path as the source. Step five: unarchive or install the artifact on each host. Step six: once all hosts have the artifact, send a single centralized notification or run a register-only task from the controller with delegate_to: localhost and run_once to signal completion. Finally, clean up the controller's temporary directory with delegate_to: localhost and run_once if it was created. This ordered approach avoids race conditions, reduces duplicated work, and keeps controller-side state explicit.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When using delegate_to and run_once you may encounter a few common mistakes. First, confusing delegate_to with hosts: some learners attempt to move a task between plays by changing delegate_to; remember that hosts still defines the play's target list. Second, relying on implicit facts in a delegated task causes surprises: a delegated task runs on a different host and will not have the original host's facts unless you gathered and passed them. Third, not accounting for batching or serial can make run_once appear inconsistent because the first host in each batch may differ. Fourth, forgetting inventory or connection configuration for the delegated host leads to connection failures; ensure the delegated host is reachable and has proper SSH keys or connection variables. Finally, running sensitive operations on the control node without cleanup exposes secrets. Troubleshoot by checking task delegations in the playbook output, verifying registered variables, and using verbose Ansible output to confirm where tasks executed. When uncertain, reproduce the run with a small inventory and explicit serial to observe which host becomes the first in the batch. screens.title: Best practices, security, and alternatives
screens.narratorSegment: Use delegate_to sparingly and intentionally. If a task touches sensitive secrets or must run on a dedicated management host for compliance, prefer a dedicated play that targets that management host rather than repeatedly delegating from many hosts; this makes auditing and access control clearer. When delegating to localhost, minimize exposure by avoiding long-lived secrets in temporary files and by removing temporary directories after the run. Use run_once to reduce duplicated work, but be mindful of inventory ordering; combine run_once with an explicit delegate_to when you need the one-time task to run on a specific host. For higher reliability, consider separate plays: create the artifact on a control-node play that runs once, then start a separate play that targets the webservers to fetch and install that artifact. This clear separation improves readability and reduces subtle variable or batch ordering bugs. Always document delegation choices in your playbook so future maintainers understand which host is the actor and which is the subject of the operation. screens.narratorSegment: These three key concepts summarize how delegation and single-run tasks shape orchestration. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore how Ansible can run a task somewhere other than the host you are currently iterating over. You will learn the purpose of delegated execution and the common patterns that rely on it, such as running control-node build steps, updating external services, or ensuring a single centralized action after a multi-host deployment. We will also show how run_once limits a task to a single execution in a batch, why inventory and delegated host variables differ, and how to use delegate_to: localhost as the modern replacement for local_action. These capabilities let you orchestrate complex workflows: prepare artifacts on the control node, copy them to many targets, and send one notification from the controller. As you learn, notice the safety and variable considerations, and how run_once interacts with batching or serial execution. By the end you will understand when to delegate, when to run locally, and when to prefer separate plays instead of delegation.

By the end of this chapter you will have four concrete skills. First, you will understand the purpose of delegated execution: why and when you would run a task on a host other than the current target. This matters because many orchestration steps, like interacting with cloud APIs or updating a load balancer, must run from a host that has the right access or tools. Second, you will be able to use delegate_to correctly to run a single task on another host, and you will know inventory and connectivity requirements for the delegated host. Third, you will implement run_once so tasks execute only a single time per batch; you will learn how batching and serial execution affect which host runs that single task. Fourth, you will perform local control-node actions using delegate_to: localhost or local_action and know the security and cleanup considerations for these patterns. Each skill includes a practical example or mnemonic so you can see how to apply it in real playbooks.

This screen outlines applied objectives tied to a hands-on delegated deployment scenario. You will create a local build directory on the control node and simulate packaging, then distribute that artifact to every web server. You will practice copying files from the control node to remote hosts, unarchiving remotely, and finally sending a single centralized notification from the control node using run_once. Each objective clarifies the why: building locally ensures deterministic artifacts, copying from localhost avoids external storage, and a single notification avoids duplicated alerts. We also cover cleanup of local temporary files and the safe use of delegated state, so you avoid leaving artifacts or secrets on the controller. These tasks map directly to the hands-on activity and prepare you to validate results on both controller and remote hosts. Learning Objectives — Applied Practice means practice building locally, distributing artifacts, and triggering a single post-deploy action from the control node.. In practical terms, how you will demonstrate these skills in a real workflow. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Delegated execution means running a specific Ansible task on a different host than the play's current target. This is useful when the action requires tools, credentials, or network access that the original target does not have. For example, you might run cloud A P I calls from a management server, update a load balancer from the load balancer host, or create artifacts on the control node before copying them out. The directive delegate_to is the mechanism that instructs Ansible to open a connection to another host and execute the task there. Delegation keeps the play focused on the inventory host list so the loop semantics and registered variables remain consistent. Importantly, variables like inventory_hostname and ansible_host continue to refer to the original target, while ansible_delegated_host points to the host where the task actually ran. A common misconception is believing delegate_to changes the play's target; it does not. It only changes the execution context for that single task. Think of delegation as borrowing a worker to perform one job on behalf of the current target. When you plan orchestration, ask which host holds the necessary tools and where state should be recorded before deciding to delegate.

The delegate_to directive tells Ansible to establish a connection to the named host and run the task there. For this to work the delegated host must be reachable from the control node and should be present in the inventory with the necessary connection variables. When Ansible executes a delegated task, it does not change the play's iteration target: the play still moves through the original hosts, and registered variables like inventory_hostname continue to refer to those original hosts. In the delegated task you gain access to a special variable, ansible_delegated_host, which holds the name of the host that actually executed the command. This distinction matters when you need to refer to facts of the original target versus the executor. For example, you might want to use the original host IP to register with a DNS service while performing the registration call from a management host. A frequent pitfall is assuming delegate_to will inherit facts from the original host; it will not. If you need facts from the original host within a delegated action, gather them beforehand and pass them as variables to the delegated task. Always confirm inventory entries and SSH keys for the delegated host before relying on delegation in production.

Understanding which variable refers to which host is essential when delegating tasks. inventory_hostname always points to the host that the play is iterating over, the host Ansible is conceptually managing in that task iteration. ansible_host typically holds the address used to contact that original host. When you delegate a task, the execution happens on a different machine; Ansible exposes ansible_delegated_host to indicate the actual executor. Use inventory_hostname and ansible_host when you need data about the original target, for example the IP address you want to register. Use ansible_delegated_host if you need to know where the command ran, for example to log execution location or to use facts from the delegated host. A common mistake is swapping these accidentally and recording the wrong host into an external system. If your task registers information about the original target, explicitly reference inventory_hostname or ansible_host in templates or A P I calls, even inside a delegated task. This clear separation prevents mixing up who is the subject of the action and who is the actor. Variables: inventory_hostname vs ansible_delegated_host means inventory_hostname and ansible_host describe the original target; ansible_delegated_host names the host that executed the task.. In practical terms, why these variables differ and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The run_once directive tells Ansible to execute a task only once within the current batch of hosts. If you target multiple hosts in a single play, a task with run_once: true runs only for the first host in that batch. This behavior is particularly useful for tasks that must run a single time, such as generating a unique deployment ID, creating a global resource, or sending an external notification. When combined with delegate_to, run_once controls how many times the delegated action happens: you can delegate a single notification to the control node and ensure it only runs once, for example. A key subtlety is that run_once is applied per batch, and batching changes the identity of the first host. If you use serial or a dynamic inventory, the first host may differ between runs, so plan accordingly. A common misconception is expecting run_once to run on a fixed host across runs; instead it runs on the first host seen in the current execution ordering. If you need a specific host to run a one-time task always, explicitly delegate_to that host and include run_once to avoid accidental repeats.

Historically Ansible provided local_action as a shorthand to run a task on the control node. Today, delegate_to: localhost is the preferred and more explicit approach. Both achieve the same effect: the task executes on the control node, which is useful for creating local build artifacts, calling local tools, or performing cleanup. The advantage of delegate_to: localhost is consistent syntax with other delegate_to uses and clearer intent when scanning a playbook. When running locally, remember the control node's security posture: tasks executed there have access to local files and credentials. Also, local_action or delegate_to: localhost will not magically copy remote facts to the controller; if you need facts from remote hosts while running local operations, gather them first and pass them explicitly. A mistake students often make is assuming local actions are isolated; in reality they can expose secrets or leave temporary files on the control node if you do not clean them up. Use run_once with delegate_to: localhost when you want a single controller-side step in a multi-host deployment. delegate_to: localhost vs local_action means use delegate_to: localhost for control-node tasks; local_action is deprecated shorthand but both run on the controller.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The play targets webservers while creating a temporary build directory on the control node using delegate_to: localhost and run_once: true. That ensures the directory is created only once, on the controller, even though the play iterates multiple web servers. Next, a simulated copy creates a package in that directory again delegated to the control node. Notice the tasks that run on remote hosts do not use delegate_to and run on each webserver. The play sets facts based on a control node command that generates a deployment ID with delegate_to: localhost and run_once, then the set_fact runs on each host so they share the same ID. Finally, a centralized debug notification runs delegate_to: localhost with run_once to ensure a single, controller-sent message, and cleanup removes the temporary directory if it was created. This pattern keeps builds centralized while distributing the artifact to all targets. Use delegate_to sparingly and intentionally. If a task touches sensitive secrets or must run on a dedicated management host for compliance, prefer a dedicated play that targets that management host rather than repeatedly delegating from many hosts; this makes auditing and access control clearer. When delegating to localhost, minimize exposure by avoiding long-lived secrets in temporary files and by removing temporary directories after the run. Use run_once to reduce duplicated work, but be mindful of inventory ordering; combine run_once with an explicit delegate_to when you need the one-time task to run on a specific host. For higher reliability, consider separate plays: create the artifact on a control-node play that runs once, then start a separate play that targets the webservers to fetch and install that artifact. This clear separation improves readability and reduces subtle variable or batch ordering bugs. These three key concepts summarize how delegation and single-run tasks shape orchestration. Delegated Execution lets you run a specific task on a different host so actions happen where tools, credentials, or network access are available. Use delegate_to for this behavior and refer to ansible_delegated_host when you need to know the executor. run_once ensures a task runs only once per batch; combine it with delegate_to when you want a single centralized action from a particular executor. Finally, prefer delegate_to: localhost over local_action for running control-node tasks, but treat controller actions carefully: secure the node, clean up artifacts, and consider using a separate play for auditable or sensitive steps. Keep variable responsibilities clear: inventory_hostname and ansible_host remain the subject; ansible_delegated_host is the actor.
